utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Good morning. Have the accused brought in, please, Mr. Registrar. (The accused entered court)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Good morning to the interpreters. I want to be sure that everybody can hear me. Good morning to the parties, to the accused as well. I would like to tell you the following. Mr. Kehoe, I would like to make a short announcement first. Thank you. It has to do with our schedule. In agreement with my colleague and my friend, Judge Shahabuddeen, we have decided, since tomorrow there are no hearings for official reasons, I would like to say that we would like to finish with this witness, and then this afternoon, if necessary, we will set up a Status Conference which will be closed to the public in order to review as completely as possible all the effects of the fact that our friend and colleague, Judge Riad, is not available. After having heard what you have to say, we will probably not take a decision at the bench, but we'll reflect on it, and I would like already to ask you to think about all the possibilities. It's been understood that the rights of the accused must be taken into account and to resolve this problem which is unusual for us. We're not going to speak about it in public. I'm going to ask the witness to be brought in, I think that will take some of the morning, and if we have the time, we'll do the Status Conference this morning, but we'll resume the 71 hearings on Thursday morning and Thursday afternoon and then Friday in the morning, as had been scheduled. I may say this so that the Defence can prepare itself. But before that, in light of next week's schedule, we have to have a meeting together about all the effects of this new situation. Having said this, I would like to give the floor back to Mr. Kehoe who apparently wanted to make a statement and whom I interrupted, I would like to apologise, and now he can tell us what he wanted to say.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Good morning, Mr. President. Good morning, Judge Shahabuddeen and Counsel. Yesterday, when I stood up to begin my cross, I neglected to introduce to the Court the new courtroom deputy and case manager that has joined the Blaskic team after this period of time, the gentleman seated to my left, Mr. Andrew Powell, and I apologise for not making those introductions yesterday, both to the Court, Counsel, and to Mr. Powell, but I suppose better later than never.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: I think I can speak for Judge Shahabuddeen to tell you that we can really excuse you for that omission. Very well. We would like to welcome your assistant. We can now have the witness brought in. Mr. Palavra, I believe that is his name. Mr. Palavra. (The witness entered court)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Mr. Palavra, do you hear me? Please be seated. Please be seated. We can now continue with the cross-examination conducted by the Prosecutor. Let me remind you that you are still under oath. Mr. Kehoe, you may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Cross-examined by Mr. Kehoe: (Cont'd)

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Good morning, Colonel. Let me show you, as we begin, I can first show you a document that we can move into, and if I can give these to the courtroom deputy Thomas. These are a few preliminary questions, Colonel, I would like to ask you before we move into the rest of the cross-examination and where we left off yesterday, so if I can digress just a few moments before we get back into that.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: This is D562.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, Colonel, this is a decoration that you received in 1996 by President Franjo Tudjman of the Republic of Croatia, and for reference purposes, I believe your name is 61; is that right? You have to respond orally into the microphone, sir.

utterances.speaker: MARINKO PALAVRA
utterances.text: Yes, yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And, Colonel, this is for outstanding wartime achievement for the good of the Republic of Croatia; is that right? I refer you to the front page where it says, "Decision conferring on the following, the Order of the Croatian," and pardon my pronunciation, "Trefoil for the outstanding wartime achievement for the good of the Republic of Croatia"; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO PALAVRA
utterances.text: Your Honours, you know that when the cease-fire was signed, that is to say, the agreement was signed in Split between Alija Izetbegovic, that is to say, Franjo Tudjman, the President of the Croatian state and the then member of the presidency, the president of Bosnia-Herzegovina, an agreement was signed and that Croatian forces could be active in the region of Bosnia-Herzegovina, and that agreement was signed. As we were a component of the HVO, I am very pleased to have been decorated by the president of all the Croats, and nothing can be contested here, as far as I'm concerned.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, Colonel, did you act in conjunction with Croatian forces?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO PALAVRA
utterances.text: Yes, we acted after the signing of this cease-fire, this agreement, which means that there was the Kupres operation, Glamoc, and Grahovo, and everything that came after the signing of the agreement, that is to say, after the signing of the cease-fire.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, which cease-fire are you talking about, sir?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO PALAVRA
utterances.text: I am talking about the fact that we participated from the time that the agreement was signed, that is to say, between the Croatian state and the Croatian army and the forces, that is to say, that they could be active in Bosnia-Herzegovina from the Kupres operation onwards.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When was that, sir?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO PALAVRA
utterances.text: It was after the signing of the cease-fire in 1994.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The individuals that received this Order of the Croatian Trefoil, were they all Croats?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO PALAVRA
utterances.text: I don't know. Let me see. Yes, they were all Croats.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, do you know a man by the name of Anto Furundzija?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO PALAVRA
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And who is Mr. Furundzija?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO PALAVRA
utterances.text: Mr. Furundzija was a member of the light battalion. He was a subordinate commander. He was not actually a commander. He was not a senior officer in that unit.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did he receive a similar award as you, this exact award, the Order of the Croatian Trefoil?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO PALAVRA
utterances.text: I don't know, possibly, because at that time, he did take part in the activities of the joint forces from Kupres onwards, Glamoc, Livno, et cetera, and he probably did. I don't know what order he received, but it is possible that he did because he was in the Special Purposes Unit of the civilian police at that time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let me show you Prosecutor's Exhibit 547.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And 547, Mr. President and Judge Shahabuddeen, is the Order of the Croatian Trefoil that was awarded to Mr. Holman, at number 143, and I would like to show this same document because on that page at 132, it reflects the name of Anto Furundzija.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Is it important for you, Mr. Kehoe, to refer to these decorations that were given to other people other than the accused? I don't want us to use up too much time here. If you say "yes," well, then, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: It will. I will tie it up, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: All right. Very well.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Colonel, take a look at that, and if you can page through that, I will direct your attention to 132 which is the second page in, and that reflects Anto Furundzija's name as receiving this same award; is that correct? You have to answer audibly, sir, "yes" or "no." You have to say "yes" into the microphone or "no" into the microphone.

utterances.speaker: MARINKO PALAVRA
utterances.text: Yes, yes, that's what it says here, "Anto Furundzija, soldier of the special police of the MUP of Croatia," et cetera.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: I think my learned counsel there is correct. I think that the microphone can be turned a little bit towards him, sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: The usher needs to assist the witness so he sits in the right position and the microphone is directed towards his face so that he can be comfortable and he can testify without having to crawl up onto the desk to be audible. Thank you. Could you do that, please?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: I think that the witness is big enough to assume the responsibility about knowing how he has to sit at the table. Try to relax, Mr. Palavra. It is true that you have to try to answer clearly, distinctly. You are before Judges, before a Tribunal, and you have nothing to fear. Try to relax a bit, take your time, and then answer clearly into the microphone so that everybody can hear, first of all, the interpreters, actually. All right. Go ahead.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Colonel, this is the same Anto Furundzija who was the head of the Jokeri and also was the head of a 3rd Light Assault Battalion; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO PALAVRA
utterances.text: I do not know that. I wasn't there at the time. I came to the military police of the 4th Battalion on the 1st of August, 1993, but I do know that Anto Furundzija was never a senior official in the Jokers, and I know the schematic of that. I know that Vlado Cosic was the commander and not Furundzija, as far as I know, that is.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Colonel, when you came to take over the 4th military police battalion in the beginning of August, 1993, Anto Furundzija was in the 3rd Light Assault Battalion, wasn't he?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO PALAVRA
utterances.text: Yes, but not at the beginning of 1993. I took over my duties on the 1st of August, 1993, and before that, that is to say, before the 1st of August, 1993, the commander of the military police was Pasko Ljubicic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And prior to the light assault battalion, Anto Furundzija was in the Jokers, wasn't he?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO PALAVRA
utterances.text: I don't know. I was in Travnik at the time. I really don't know because I did not do research into his wartime biography, but I do know the man.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay, sir, we'll change subjects now, and I'd like to talk to you about some of your testimony during direct examination concerning the transfer of your personnel, your Special Purposes Unit, from Travnik, I believe you came to the area of Kraljevica or Bukovica; is that right? You have to say "yes" or "no," sir. Is that correct? Sir, you have to answer verbally, "yes" or "no," because the transcript will only show --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Mr. Palavra, you must answer. The interpreters can see you, and they indicate that you're nodding, but we don't work with sign language here. These are oral proceedings. Criminal proceedings are, in principal, oral. You can say "yes," "no," "perhaps." You can give explanations, but you must answer. I'm asking you for the last time.

utterances.speaker: MARINKO PALAVRA
utterances.text: While I was the commander of the Special Purposes Unit in Travnik, the unit for special purposes attached to the police department in Travnik, I left last with my unit from the central section of Travnik, although before me, other people had left, that is to say, the command of the Travnik brigade. Everybody had left Travnik and went towards Kalburnada (phoen) and the borders of the Travnik municipality. Having left Travnik, I went to Kraljevica with my unit because the chief of police of Travnik was there at Kraljevica. I stayed there up until the Croats were expelled from Travnik, and I was able to pull out with my unit, that is to say, part of the unit, in the region of the Lasva River Valley under the control of the Croats, and part of the unit, another part of the unit, was made up of the wounded which we had, and they went via Vlasic, Mount Vlasic, and the soldiers who died were buried in Travnik. That is my answer.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, the wounded that went by way of Vlasic, did they go through Serb lines?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO PALAVRA
utterances.text: Yes, yes, they did go via Serb lines. Not only them, but everybody went via Serb lines.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And when did this take place?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO PALAVRA
utterances.text: It took place in June.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Early June, late June, could you give us an approximation, if you can?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO PALAVRA
utterances.text: I think that it was the beginning of June.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So the activities of the HVO in moving wounded and other people up through Vlasic, those activities were coordinated between the HVO and the army of the Republika Srpska or the VRS; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO PALAVRA
utterances.text: I don't know about that, whether it was coordinated or not. I know that there were attacks by Muslims all the time in the Travnik municipality, and the positions which the HVO had and held were under constant attack from the Muslim forces, especially the Mujahedin units and the units of the 7th Muslim Brigade, part of it. So that at that time, I did not make the decisions. They had probably arrived at some sort of solution. Whatever that was, it was not mine because I was a soldier at that time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, sir, you were, in fact, at that time, a leader of the Special Purposes Unit in the police, weren't you? You weren't just some soldier on the street. You were running a particular unit in the police department at that time, were you not?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO PALAVRA
utterances.text: Yes, yes, that's right. I am not ashamed of that. I was in Travnik --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Mr. Nobilo?

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Mr. President, my learned colleague has entered into a region which was not comprised in the examination-in-chief. I let him go ahead with one or two questions, but I see that the direction of his cross-examination encompasses areas which were not touched on in the examination-in-chief. After biographical data, we began with the military police and the 1st of August, 1993.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: No. The last point had to do with the fact that the witness was saying that he was an ordinary soldier or that he was an official, but he can't be both at the same time. Go ahead, Mr. Kehoe, continue.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So you were an official in the police in early June 1993?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO PALAVRA
utterances.text: Yes, I was. I was the commander of the Special Purposes Unit.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you gave orders to your subordinates to transfer from Travnik to Kraljevica; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO PALAVRA
utterances.text: No. I received an order from the head of the department of the civilian police of Travnik, and at that time, the chief of police there was Mr. Ivo Rezo, so I was just following orders from the chief of the police station there to which we were attached and where he was the senior officer for the complete police force in Travnik. It was under his command.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, Colonel, given your position in the police, do you know if the HVO was consulting and coordinating with the VRS, the army of the Republika Srpska or the Bosnian Serb army?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO PALAVRA
utterances.text: I really don't know, but I think that after the civilians left Travnik and the army left Travnik towards the Serb-held territories at that time, this was decided upon by the government of the HVO, and this was under the control of the civilian authorities.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So the government of the HVO did have agreements with the army of the Republika Srpska; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO PALAVRA
utterances.text: I don't know that. You can't ask me that. I was a soldier. What the government did, I really cannot say. At that time and in the crucial moments and when the Mujahedins and the army units were attacking where the Croatian Defence Council was in control, where there was a Croatian army and civilians, there was burning, there was a lot of destruction, there was a slaughtering, there was a takeover of territory, and quite normally, they made decisions in those crucial times to save lives because you must not forget that Travnik, the ratio was one to eight to the advantage of the Muslim units.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, how many Bosnian Croats crossed over Serb lines?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO PALAVRA
utterances.text: I don't know how many, but there were civilians. There were 20-odd, 25.000, 26.000 in Travnik, and of that number, 2.000 Croats remained. The rest had to flee, and all the military-able men I know did cross over because they said so. They said that there were about 800 to 1.000 later on, I don't know exactly, military-able men transferred to Serb territory. The others were children, the elderly, the infirm, the wounded, and so on. I don't know the exact figures. I did not determine their route towards Serb territory. I just set out towards the territory under HVO control, although I thought that we were in an encirclement at that time, and Bukovica was free at the time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Colonel, the Kiseljak area was also part of the Central Bosnian Operative Zone and under the command of Colonel Blaskic; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO PALAVRA
utterances.text: Yes, that's right, it was.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know of coordinated acts, coordinated military activity, between the HVO and the VRS against the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina that took place in the Kiseljak municipality in early June of 1993?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO PALAVRA
utterances.text: I do not know that, no.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, the Zepce area was also in the Central Bosnian Operative Zone and under the command of Colonel Blaskic; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO PALAVRA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know of coordinated acts, military actions by the HVO operating in conjunction with the VRS that took place in late June in the Zepce area? Are you aware of that?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO PALAVRA
utterances.text: At the end of June, but what year?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Of 1993, sir.

utterances.speaker: MARINKO PALAVRA
utterances.text: I don't know. I really don't know. At the time I was in the civilian police force in Travnik.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: You can't ask the witness to reconsider the entire war strategies. We are not here for that. He had a position in the military police. I want you to concentrate your questions or else explain to the Judges what you are trying to get from the witness. Do one thing or the other so that we can evaluate. We are now asking questions about all the military and strategic aspects of the conflict in the former Yugoslavia, and we are only receiving evasive answers, or at the best, approximate answers, so I would like things to be clearer, not to waste too much time on that. Or explain where you are trying to go.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. What is of interest during June of 1993, commencing with the testimony that was given by the Colonel, was the co-operation between the HVO and the VRS in June in the Travnik area. What we also have during that relatively same period of time, based on the testimony that Your Honours have heard, are coordinated military activities and artillery attack support provided by the VRS to the HVO in the Kiseljak municipality in attacks on villages such as Han Ploca, Tulice and others. In addition to that, Your Honours also heard testimony of coordinated activity by the HVO and the VRS again in June of 1993, albeit the latter part of June of 1993 where the HVO and the VRS in coordinated activities attacked and engaged in military activities in the Zepce area. The common denominator for all of this, Mr. President and Judge Shahabuddeen, is the military commander, General Blaskic, who is the commander of Zepce area, part of the Central Bosnia Operative Zone, who is the commander of the Travnik area, also part of the Central Bosnia Operative Zone, and also the Kiseljak area, which is part of the Central Bosnia Operative Zone, where all this activity and coordination with the VRS was taking place. Likewise, Your Honours heard during the testimony of Mr. Tolo that letter that was received in evidence from a Colonel from the VRS whose name escapes me, who was talking about coordinated activity in co-operation with the HVO was, in fact, the Colonel's, Colonel Blaskic's immediate commander, when Colonel Blaskic was then Captain Blaskic in the JNA and in Slovenia. So what I was attempting to ask --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Yes, thank you. Thank you also on behalf of Judge Shahabuddeen. Thank you for the clarifications. I understand better now. But nonetheless you should focus your questions on the specific functions that the witness had. Don't forget that this witness has come at the request of the Defence to speak about his experience as a military police official.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. I was just simply asking some questions based on his direct testimony where he mentioned these wounded going up through the Vlasic feature that came out on direct. I will move onto a separate subject at this juncture.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Colonel, what I would like to do at this point is move to your initial meetings and events just prior to that initial meeting that you had with the accused, Colonel Blaskic. And you noted during your direct testimony that Blaskic was unhappy with Pasko Ljubicic who prior to that was in charge of the 4th Military Police Battalion; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO PALAVRA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you noted in your direct testimony that Pasko Ljubicic didn't follow orders; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO PALAVRA
utterances.text: I'll explain this to you once again. Let me repeat it. The military police -- I already explained this schematic -- in its organisation, I mean the administration of the police actually commanded the 4th Battalion, and in a situation of war, of course, the commander of the Operative Zone has the highest responsibility, and that is what is exactly written everywhere too. And I also know that at that time the military police was independent in its zone of responsibility, and it was not only the commander of the Operative Zone of Central Bosnia but also the commanders of the other operative zones too. My opinion is that at that time they wanted to have control over the entire area, that is to say those who were controlling it, however, the military police came into the picture, which is not commanded by the commander of the Operative Zone. Perhaps in terms of daily routines, yes, but this is where this discrepancy came about. There were some who wanted to take over total control, that is to say commanders of the operative zones, as far as I know, and there were always misunderstandings there in terms of dual leadership and command. The commander of the Operative Zone, naturally, wants to have control over everything. This is my opinion. And they wanted to -- and they would want to put everything under their command. So there was always this -- these discrepancy as to who was commanding and how. That is my opinion and that is my answer.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Colonel, my question is this: Did you say in direct examination, in response to Mr. Nobilo's questions, that Pasko Ljubicic did not follow orders? Did you say that?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO PALAVRA
utterances.text: Pasko Ljubicic, I never -- I mean, I only heard from Colonel Blaskic at the time when he received me at his command of the Operative Zone. He said that he was not satisfied with the military police as it was at that time, and that a reorganisation had to be carried out as soon as possible. He did not explain the reasons for this to me, that Pasko was this or that kind of a person. As I talked to policemen I found out -- well, they have spoken arbitrarily too, that between Colonel Blaskic at the time and Pasko, they did have some disagreements at the time and that the chain of command had broken down, precisely, allegedly, for those reasons, namely, that Colonel Blaskic at that time wanted to have control over the military police too. And Pasko wanted to keep his independence and to work according to what he thought was right and to be held responsible only by the administration of the military police. This is not only the case of the Operative Zone in Central Bosnia. The other operative zones had the same kind of situation. Again, there was this discrepancy, as I said, that is to say this dual command, because the commanders of the units of the military police wanted to be somebody too in the zone of responsibility because the minister gave this right to them or, rather, the chief of the head office of the military police. And, on the other hand, these units of the military police and of the security were under the direct command of the Minister of Defence. That is what I wish to say.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Colonel, on page 16717, starting on line 4, you were asked this question by my learned colleague,

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: "What happened between Pasko Ljubicic and Colonel Blaskic? What happened between the two?" Answer: "I do not know what happened between the two, but Pasko wanted to retain the hierarchy, to retain his command over the military police, and did not, in fact, follow orders." My question to you is: What orders did Pasko Ljubicic not follow?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO PALAVRA
utterances.text: Well, I don't know. I don't know, but probably orders from the commander of the Operative Group or Zone. I don't know. I really don't know. At that time I wasn't there, but I only know from the moment when I took over on the 1st of August 1993 that all orders and everything that happened in the Operative Zone I carried out all orders. Why? Because I realised that we Croats could not act differently. One person wants to do this, the other person wants to do that. We have to subordinate everything to our defence. Our units were under attack every day and I wasn't thinking at all whether it was this way or that way. The important thing was to save peoples lives and that is the way all of us at headquarters behaved. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, Colonel, did you refuse any orders given to you by Colonel Blaskic?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO PALAVRA
utterances.text: No. At that time I did not. But we always consulted what should be done, whether it should be done this way or that way, and once we agreed, then I would transmit this to my subordinates, to company commanders, et cetera. But there was always agreement, but I never refused. Why would I refuse? Because everything was fair, in my opinion.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did these orders that came from Colonel Blaskic include written and oral orders?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO PALAVRA
utterances.text: Depends on the situation. There were written orders and there were also oral orders. It depends on the circumstances involved, the circumstances that we were in at the time, but most of the time -- the main point is that there was coordination.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, Colonel, when you -- going back to Pasko Ljubicic. When you told the Trial Chamber that Pasko Ljubicic did not in fact follow orders, am I correct in saying that you don't know what orders Pasko Ljubicic refused to follow?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO PALAVRA
utterances.text: You are right, I don't know. At that time I wasn't there, but I assume, and in these conversations with the military policemen -- well, I described the situation to you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In fact, Pasko Ljubicic was promoted, wasn't he?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO PALAVRA
utterances.text: I don't understand.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: He received a promotion from his job in the 4th Military Police Battalion to the assistant head of security for Central Bosnia; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO PALAVRA
utterances.text: Try to imagine this situation. Probably, I don't know. But just try to imagine this situation. The commander of the 4th Battalion of the military police is being replaced, a new commander comes in. As things unravel, at that time the head office of the military police assessed that it would be right for Pasko to be some kind of coordinator up there in Central Bosnia for the military police, because he was the only one who knew the position and who knew the situation. And now it is up to the administration, the head office of the military police, to decide what they will decide. And then the 4th Battalion of the military police, all of this was up to me, and I had to do everything, all the operative work involved. Pasko just read reports, nothing else. I mean, he was there at the hotel.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, Colonel, how long did Pasko Ljubicic remain in his position as the assistant head of security in Central Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO PALAVRA
utterances.text: Well, look, it wasn't only Pasko Ljubicic who was assistant chief. At that time the head of the police administration appointed three or four assistant chiefs, because the area was fragmented and the military police could not -- could not be unified. It was fragmented. So in order to have a better situation at work and in order to coordinate activities, Pasko was, for example, appointed over there, and his only zone of responsibility was only in that area and not in the entire area covered by the military police. And Pasko was there about a month, I am not too sure, a month or two, I can't say exactly, but he was supposed to leave even before that. But as soon as I came to the 4th Battalion, on the 1st of October 1993, Pasko was supposed to go to military police headquarters, but since we were encircled, I think that he left by helicopter, because I am not sure when helicopters could fly, but I know that he was supposed to leave and it was postponed from one day to another. But, I don't know, he wasn't there for longer than a month and a half in this particular area.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So would you say by mid-September Pasko Ljubicic was gone, or September 1?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO PALAVRA
utterances.text: I don't know. I have an agenda at home where I have all flights registered, so I cannot remember now when Pasko left, but at any rate Pasko did leave the area of Central Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When he was there and you were there, you answered to Pasko Ljubicic and took orders from Pasko Ljubicic, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO PALAVRA
utterances.text: Pasko spent a very short period of time in the area of Central Bosnia. From my arrival that is. At first he would go to the early morning briefings, Pasko Ljubicic would go to General Blaskic and then Pasko would convey to me all the things that had to be done by the military police and what their assignments were. However, this lasted for a very short time, because at the time Pasko would either come to the Operative Zone or would be detained, I don't know where, and then Colonel Blaskic would call me afterwards to these meetings because we had regular briefings every week. On Fridays we would all report to the commander of the Operative Zone, everybody, all the commanders, and naturally that included the commander of the 4th Battalion of the military police too.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When Ljubicic was the assistant chief, was his office in the Hotel Vitez?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO PALAVRA
utterances.text: Yes, yes. His office was in the Vitez hotel.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Colonel, you mentioned that there were several assistant chiefs. How many assistant chiefs were located in the Hotel Vitez, other than Ljubicic?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO PALAVRA
utterances.text: Obviously, you did not understand my answer. The head, the chief of the administration of the military police, of the head office of the military police in Ljubusko, he appointed his assistants in the territory of Central Bosnia, and in that area Pasko Ljubicic was the assistant chief, and also in the area of southeast Herzegovina or southwest Herzegovina, and in Posavina, he had his assistant chiefs in all these areas, in all these parts of Bosnia-Herzegovina that were under the control of or, rather, where there was HVO military police. That is to say that Pasko was only assistant chief for the area of Central Bosnia, and his office was in the Vitez hotel.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, after he received the job as assistant chief of security for Central Bosnia, did he receive another promotion when he went down to Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO PALAVRA
utterances.text: No. He was not appointed assistant chief of security. He was assistant chief of military police, not of security. After leaving Lasva River Valley, Pasko spent some time at the head office of the military police. For a very short period of time he stayed there, and he went to the MUP, that is to say he went to the civilian police, to the civilian police of Herceg-Bosna at the time, its headquarters being in Mostar, and he did not spend much time in the military police, only a very short period of time after he left the Lasva River Valley.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let's shift gears, Colonel, if we will. Let's go back to this first meeting that you had with Blaskic in early August of 1993. Now, in this meeting, I think you said in your testimony yesterday, that Blaskic told you that you had the most responsible job in the Operative Zone; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO PALAVRA
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And he also told you that as part of your job, in the reformation of the military police, was to make it a national police; is that correct? In other words, a police that was responsive to the Bosnian Serbs, the Bosnians Croats, as well as the Bosnian Muslims?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO PALAVRA
utterances.text: No, no, that's not the way it was. Colonel Blaskic said -- I remember this meeting very well -- that this was a military police of the people, that is to say it is not that there are Croats, Serbs, Muslims, and that they would take care of only one part of the population or act against one part of the population. That is to say that all peoples who lived under HVO control are citizens and should be treated as such, and they are all the same before the law, and that there should be no separations of this kind, no Serbs, Muslims, Croats, whatever. In the units of the military police I truly did have some Muslims there too. I had -- I can tell you straightaway, I can even give you the name of Adis Cosic, who was an exemplary man in the military police units. Until the present day he has remained in our territories and he works there too. Also there were quite a few Serbs and there was never a national ethnic criterion involved, who would join the police. In Central Bosnia, it was a popular police, a police of the people, and there were Croats, Serbs, Muslims, and what have you. And he also said that in our area there were UNPROFOR units too, that these were people who came. They are also someone's children, somebody sent them too. Also representatives of the UNHCR, the Red Cross, the European monitors. All of these are people who came with their own assignments, and it is precisely in our interest for them to see the real situation in the Lasva River Valley, because we are the ones who an encircled, we are the ones who are attacked, and it is in our interest for the people to see the actual state of affairs. And he said that we had to defend and protect their property and their people at every point in time, and if they were attacked by anyone. I remember that's exactly what he said. And I, of course, agreed with him and said that that is the way it was, because indeed at that time we needed to show the world the real situation that prevailed in that area. There was no food, there were no clothes, there was no footwear, there were many displaced persons, many civilians. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Colonel, when you took over in August of 1993, how many Muslims were there in HVO controlled area?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO PALAVRA
utterances.text: I really don't know. There are facts about this, but I really don't know. My task was to organise and lead the units of the military police, but I do know that there were Muslims as well, a lot, of considerable number. I know that there were Serbs as well in units from -- going from Novi Travnik, Busovaca, Vitez, and so on. And there are documents on that score. I know that there was a considerable number.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You just noted in your testimony, Colonel, that your job was to protect and defend everybody; is that right? How many people did you arrest for attacking Bosnian Muslims, burning their houses, stealing from them, looting from them, or committing any crimes against Bosnian Muslims? How many did you arrest during your tenure from 1 August 1993 until the Washington Peace Accords were signed, or thereafter? How many?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO PALAVRA
utterances.text: Well, I don't know if you have a particular fact on -- on the fact that a Muslim had been arrested or a Serb expelled or that he was maltreated by the military police or the HVO. At that time, on the 1st of August 1993, it was chaos, pure -- sheer chaos. There was so frequent attacks by Muslim units that nobody even thought of this. They just wanted to escape alive and prevent the attacks. And we were all one. Nobody looked at anything. I know that Colonel Blaskic, I can't remember exactly when, but he -- but someone -- an individual was mistreated of the Muslim nationality and he proposed measures that I investigated to see what had been done and the perpetrator brought to justice. There were cases of this kind, not a lot, but there were, as this case in point that I mentioned.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How many, Colonel? You had the most responsible job, according to the accused, in the Operative Zone, and your job, according to what you just told us, was to protect Muslims, Croats and Serbs, and my question for you is: How many people did you arrest and prosecute of the Croatian ethnicity who committed crimes against Bosnian Muslims? How many? One, two, five, 100, 200, 300, 1.000? How many?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO PALAVRA
utterances.text: I don't understand you at all. What crimes? In my time, on the 1st of August 1993, there were no -- I had no notion of crimes. At the time I brought military policemen to disciplinary action. I asked the commanders of the companies to punish them in various forms -- for various things, for looting, for behaving in a non- -- in a manner not -- that doesn't correspond to how a policeman should behave. And when the military police saw that something was amiss --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Is that the question that you asked, Mr. Kehoe?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: No, it's not, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: I don't think that you are being asked whether you sanctioned any Muslim policemen. I don't believe that was Mr. Kehoe's question. Ask your question again.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: I'll repeat the question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: That was not the question that was asked.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: My question is a very simple one, Colonel, and it is this: You took over 1 August 1993. How many people of Croat ethnicity did you arrest for crimes committed against Bosnian Muslims, any crimes committed? How many did you arrest?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO PALAVRA
utterances.text: I must tell you that from the beginning of 1993, I began on the 1st of August 1993, that's when I took over my duties as commander, and that is the second half of 1993, so from that time on. Whereas in the documentation of the military police there are records on exactly how many people, military policemen were -- disciplinary action was taken against them who had gone contrary to the laws, so that I know that in the command of the battalion I had to discard two members. One was my assistant for crime investigation, because he, in fact, collaborated with some commanders, that is Kraljevic units. He had connection with the criminals there. And so automatically I suspended him from duty --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I think my question was quite clear, Mr. President, Judge Shahabuddeen, and I believe that the answer we are receiving is not responsive. I don't mean to interrupt you, Colonel. I do apologise for the interruption. But I do believe, Mr. President, that this is not a responsive answer to the question that I proposed for the second time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct. Ask your question for the third time, and I'll ask the witness to pay careful attention to the question. Yes, Mr. Nobilo.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Mr. President, I do not agree. I feel that the witness has answered. He has answered by asking the Prosecutor, what crimes were committed during my time? Not a single one. No Muslims were killed or wounded or expelled. He said that at the beginning. And by insisting further, he understands that you want him to answer about disciplinary action, but he says that crimes did not take place over the Muslims at that time during his time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Mr. Kehoe?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Colonel, is your testimony consistent with what Mr. Nobilo just said, that there were no crimes committed against Bosnian Muslims after you took control of the 4th Military Police Battalion on the 1st of August 1993? Do you agree with what Mr. Nobilo just said?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO PALAVRA
utterances.text: I do agree. Do you have any facts and figures on what you are stating?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let's turn our attention to, in part, Exhibit 433, a series of photographs on the burnings in the village of Grbavica, after it was secured by the HVO on the 7th and 8th of September 1993. Would you like to see the burning of those houses, sir?

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: I object to the form of the question, Mr. President. If Mr. Kehoe has a question, he should ask a question. He shouldn't ask the witness if he wants to have lunch, if he wants to see a photo, if he wants to go to the dance. It's inappropriate conduct by counsel.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: No, no, no. No, no. Mr. Hayman, I don't agree at all. It was very clear. Mr. Kehoe repeated Mr. Nobilo's answer and asked the witness if he agreed with what Mr. Nobilo had said, that is, that Mr. Nobilo in a way had kind of interpreted the witness's first answer. That's where we are now. And as regards that point, Mr. Kehoe is going to produce an exhibit. Let's not multiply the exhibits. Mr. Nobilo, for the last time go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Just for precision purposes, I did not say what crimes were committed, who was killed and who was expelled and houses burnt, because I know about Grbavica. So I said which Muslim was killed, wounded, expelled, because the witness said that there were no crimes, that is to say forceful conduct and crimes against individuals.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Let the Prosecution develop its exhibits in respect of the last question. Mr. Kehoe asked the witness whether he agreed with what you said, Mr. Nobilo. The witness said yes, and now Mr. Kehoe is moving on and the Judges will make their evaluation.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You took over in August of 1993. The Military District Court, the Travnik District Military Court was operating, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO PALAVRA
utterances.text: I apologise, but what date did you say?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you took over the 4th Military Police Battalion in the beginning of August 1993, the Travnik District Military Court was operating, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO PALAVRA
utterances.text: Not in Travnik, unfortunately, but it functioned in Vitez, so the headquarters were in Vitez. But it was called the District Court in Travnik, that is to say the Military Court.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The fact remains it was operating; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO PALAVRA
utterances.text: Yes, it was.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I would like to show you Exhibit -- part of 433. I am showing you 433/21 to 433/40. With the assistance of the usher, Mr. President, just by way of some recollection, we can just put them on the ELMO in seriatim as opposed to talking about them -- without showing them on the ELMO, so the audience can hear and so Your Honours can look at it as well. Again, Mr. President and Your Honours, these are the photographs that were taken during the period by -- during the period of time of the attack on Grbavica and thereafter by Captain Lee Whitworth of the Prince of Wales own regiment of Yorkshire, who was the British battalion located in Stari Bila during this period of time. If I may just go through them. Thomas, if you could put them on the ELMO in seriatim. I think the first one is 433/21. It might be easier -- that's fine. The next one is 433/22, 433/23, 433/24. You can see from that photograph, can you not, that the gentleman on the left hand has a radio with him? Do you see that? The testimony from Captain Whitworth at the time was that these houses were being looted. 433/26. It should be this one. Yes, that's it. Keep going. 433/27, 433/28, 26, 27, 433/29, 433/30, 433/31, 433/32, 433/34, 433/35, 433/366, 433/37, 38, 39, and 40. Now, Colonel. Thank you, Mr. Usher. I appreciate it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Now, be very specific in the question that you are going to ask, Mr. Kehoe.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Colonel, after Grbavica was secured by the HVO, houses were burned and looted by members of the HVO, weren't they?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO PALAVRA
utterances.text: In view of the fact that Grbavica was taken as it was taken by military means, we cannot say that the houses were looted by members of the HVO because they were up at the frontlines, the defence lines, predominantly, but I know that at that time, the refugees, who were located in Vitez, Travnik, that is to say, part of Novi Travnik, in Novi Travnik, that they went to look for space for themselves because there were two or three families living together in a house or in two or three rooms, so that they went up there and wanted to enter Grbavica, to enter the houses and to take over that space there. That's what I know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, these were Bosnian Muslim houses; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO PALAVRA
utterances.text: Not only Bosnian Muslims, but there were Serb houses and Croatian houses as well.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, Colonel, as the head of the 4th Military Police Battalion, you were responsible for investigating the crimes against those Bosnian Muslim houses, weren't you?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO PALAVRA
utterances.text: Well, yes, not only Bosnian Muslims but everybody.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: My question is, based on what I asked you previously, how many people of Bosnian Croat ethnicity were arrested or prosecuted for the crimes committed against Bosnian Muslim houses in Grbavica in September of 1993? How many?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO PALAVRA
utterances.text: Well, I don't really know the facts and figures. The Courts probably have that figure, but I really can't say. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How many were arrested then, Colonel? Your units were responsible for the arrests. How many did the military police arrest? One, five, ten, how many?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO PALAVRA
utterances.text: I don't know. I can't tell you just offhand like that, I don't know the figure, but there were arrests, and in the penitentiary in Busovaca, there were people arrested, military-able men and others. I don't know the exact figure. I can't say 5, 10, 15, 50. I really don't know. I did not prepare myself for answering that question. But there are complete documents on that score, and you can have an insight into the documents of the military police and what it did at the time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Colonel, I'm going to make this very simple. Name one Bosnian Croat that was arrested and prosecuted for the crimes that took place against Bosnian Muslim homes in Grbavica after or on the 8th of September or 7th of September, 1993? Name one.

utterances.speaker: MARINKO PALAVRA
utterances.text: I can't answer that question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: You can't answer because you don't have the documents?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO PALAVRA
utterances.text: I don't have the documentation. I can't because I haven't got the documents here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: We're going to take a break in any case. Perhaps you can think about it. It's a legitimate question, Mr. Palavra. You had a position of responsibility which would not exclude this question being asked by either one of the parties. All right. I suggest that we take a 20-minute break, and we'll resume at twenty to twelve.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: We can now resume the hearing. Have the accused brought in, please. (The accused entered court)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Mr. Kehoe, you have the floor. I'd like to know whether you still have many questions you want to ask so that we can organise our work.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: I'm trying to move through this as fast as I possibly can, Mr. President. It's just taking a little bit more time than I'd anticipated.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, Colonel, just going back to Grbavica, was the 4th Military Police Battalion involved in the attack on Grbavica on the 7th and 8th of September of 1993?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO PALAVRA
utterances.text: The military police did not take part in the attack on Grbavica, no.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did the 3rd Light Assault Battalion, which was formerly the Jokers, take part in the attack on Grbavica?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO PALAVRA
utterances.text: I don't know, probably did, special unit -- my parts of the military police were not engaged in the Grbavica operation.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did the Vitezovi take part in the Grbavica operation?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO PALAVRA
utterances.text: They say that they were. In which parts, I don't know, but that's what was being said, but the 4th Battalion of the military police did not take part.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, to your knowledge, Colonel Blaskic ordered the attack on Grbavica on the 7th and 8th of September, 1993; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO PALAVRA
utterances.text: I don't know. I was surprised by that action too. I just know that there was this action on Grbavica, and I had no idea. I don't know. Whether it was secret or not, I don't know, probably was, but I didn't know about it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, you told us during your direct examination that it was general knowledge that members of the Vitezovi, as well as the military police, were criminals; do you recall that testimony?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO PALAVRA
utterances.text: I do. I said part of the Vitezovi unit, part of the Vitezovi unit was out of control or, rather, was under the direct protection of their commander at the time, now he is the late Kraljevic, but quite a few units were regular, so there were those who were under his protection, perhaps 20 or so men, they were under his direct protection. So at that time, that's the way it was, of course, until I came to the 4th Battalion where I tried or, rather, did carry out the reorganisation of the military police and when we started clearing up everything, starting from military policemen and going through all the units. All of those who had committed any criminal offences or who were committing any criminal offences at that time, I wanted them to be arrested immediately, and I wanted proceedings to be initiated against them so that we could see finally whether this would lead to punishment.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, if it was common knowledge that there were members of the Vitezovi who were criminals, and if the Vitezovi was involved in the attack on Grbavica on the 7th and 8th of September, 1993, what steps did Colonel Blaskic or what orders did Colonel Blaskic give to you as commander of the 4th Military Police Battalion to prevent the burning of Bosnian Muslim houses and to prevent the looting of those houses after the attack? What orders did Blaskic give?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO PALAVRA
utterances.text: During the action itself, I mean, on Grbavica, a certain number of houses were set fire to or, rather, I mean, the houses were on fire during these combat operations. A number of houses, a considerable number of houses, were on fire during the action itself because this was during the fighting, of course. However, when Grbavica was taken and when the units that took part in taking the area of Grbavica moved further on towards the Muslim forces, towards Sadovace and even further than that on the frontline, at that moment, when it was obvious that that's the way it was, the civilians got in from all sides. Civilians who were expelled from Zenica, from Travnik, from all parts, they ran into the Grbavica village. So the units moved on further towards the Muslim units, and I remember -- oh, well, I can't give you the exact number now, but there was a very large number of civilians, and also there were a military-aged man or two among them who got into the village then. So when an area is liberated, then it is civilians, and it is the civilian police that is in charge, I mean, of the entire population that is in that particular area.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you present when this burning and looting was taking place, Colonel?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO PALAVRA
utterances.text: No, no, I wasn't. I was down there in Vitez, and had I seen this or had any of my military policemen seen this, we would have taken measures, of course, but I hadn't seen this.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So if a captain from the British battalion testified that it was, in fact, soldiers who were doing this burning and looting, you would have no way of refuting that, would you, because you weren't there?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO PALAVRA
utterances.text: Yes, I was not there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Take a look at, if I can go back, with your assistance, Mr. Usher, Exhibit 433/24, if you can put that on the ELMO, Mr. Usher. Do those look like soldiers to you, Colonel?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO PALAVRA
utterances.text: Yes, it does look like soldiers.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you think that soldier on the left carrying that big radio brought it with him into battle or do you think he stole it?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO PALAVRA
utterances.text: A picture can represent anything. Perhaps he did steal it but perhaps he found it and perhaps he was taking it from one place to another, but I hadn't seen this picture before, and I see this soldier carrying a cassette player, and why, I really don't know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So I go back to my initial question, Colonel: What orders did Blaskic give to you, as commander of the 4th Military Police Battalion, to go to Grbavica after it was secured to prevent the unnecessary burning of Bosnian Muslim houses and to prevent the looting of those houses? What orders did Blaskic give, if he gave any?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO PALAVRA
utterances.text: Specifically, as far as Grbavica is concerned, I did not receive any orders, but, again, I repeat, it is civilians who got into Grbavica, and they -- I mean, yes, there truly was looting. Some people were carrying beds, and I see, yes, somebody was carrying a cassette player, somebody was probably carrying a radio too, somebody was taking wood, firewood; however, it is undeniable that there was looting, but I'm telling you that, at that time, a lot of civilians flooded into Grbavica, and some of them sought accommodation there and actually came to stay at some of these places, and others were looting these houses. So, again, I say it is civilian structures, the civilian police, who were responsible for --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Don't repeat yourself. The Judges heard your answer, and we can now have the Prosecutor move to another question.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Mr. President, my question was, did he receive any orders from Blaskic to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: He answered. He answered. He answered that he did not receive any orders for Grbavica.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: That's all right. I'll move on.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, you noted during this meeting in --

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: If I may just consult with my colleague just one second.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, you noted during this meeting that you had with Blaskic, this initial meeting that you had in August of 1993, that Blaskic told you that part of your task was to clean up the military police and to get rid of the criminal elements in the military police; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO PALAVRA
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who were the criminals in the military police that he asked you to get rid of?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO PALAVRA
utterances.text: They were members of the military police.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What were their names?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO PALAVRA
utterances.text: I wasn't going to mention them, but if necessary, no problem, I will. My assistant for crime investigation, Josipovic, Ivan Josipovic, my assistant, he was my assistant, and he directly cooperated with criminals, and he told them exactly what the military police would do and were doing, so they knew at the time because they were working together. Then also Zoran Curak, he was in my headquarters, and he had committed a criminal offence according to the Criminal Code, and he was supposed to be held accountable for it, and I eliminated him immediately, and then Policeman Gugic. I don't know. There were quite a few of them who stole things, and the military police discovered that they had stolen certain things from the area that they were providing security for. So first, naturally, they were sent to Kaonik, disciplinary action was taken against them, and then they were expelled from the military police, and they were sent to the general military office so that they could be sent to other units. That's it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Any of the individuals that you removed from the military police, were they convicted of crimes that they committed against Bosnian Muslims, and if so, give us their names and the crime that they were convicted of or charged with.

utterances.speaker: MARINKO PALAVRA
utterances.text: I cannot recall. It wasn't only Muslims. All the people who lived in this area, these policemen did more in terms of Croats. I don't know whether there is a single deed that was committed from the 1st of August, 1993 that a Serb, a Muslim, or whoever was killed or expelled and that the military police did not react or did not take action or impose sanctions. I would like to see proof of this because I do not remember any such thing.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, Colonel, you were responsible for prosecuting and investigating crimes that took place prior to you taking office; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO PALAVRA
utterances.text: The military police, yes, is responsible in terms of its tasks and responsibilities for preparing evidence for the court and also for preparing criminal reports.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Then I go back to my question: What crimes against members of the military police did you file charges on or have arrested for crimes committed against Bosnian Muslims? Tell us what you did, how many you did, and who you arrested.

utterances.speaker: MARINKO PALAVRA
utterances.text: I can't tell you the exact number, but there were cases, and they were arrested. I haven't got the facts and figures. The military courts have exact data on this, who, when, and what was done, but I really can't tell you. I really can't answer that question with any precision at this point.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, Colonel, you also said it was common knowledge that the Vitezovi was filled with criminals; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO PALAVRA
utterances.text: Not only the Vitezovi but the others as well.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What crimes did the Vitezovi commit and who committed them?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO PALAVRA
utterances.text: I can't give you the names exactly now and what crimes. They took cars, seized cars. There were brawls of various kinds where public law and order was disturbed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you ever prosecute a member of the Vitezovi for killing a Bosnian Muslim, for burning his house, for looting his house, or for driving that Bosnian Muslim out of his premises? Did you ever prosecute a member of the Vitezovi for that at any time?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO PALAVRA
utterances.text: Yes, we did prosecute them, but I can't tell you the names and surnames. I was the commander, and these names were sent to me, but that is correct, we did do that, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So you don't remember any members of the military police, you don't remember their names, and you don't remember any names of the Vitezovi who were prosecuted; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO PALAVRA
utterances.text: It's not my duty to know. The commanders of the companies told me, and there were so many figures that, quite simply, I don't know the names, but cases of this kind did exist.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, Colonel, you discussed with Blaskic in this initial meeting the fact that all these units had committed crimes; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO PALAVRA
utterances.text: Not the units but individuals, the individuals in units.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And did Blaskic know the names of these individuals in these units, the individuals who were committing crimes?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO PALAVRA
utterances.text: It was not his task. It is the task of the courts and the prosecutor's office and the military police to uncover individuals of this kind.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Colonel, did Blaskic tell you the names of criminals in these units? Did he or did he not?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO PALAVRA
utterances.text: Well, he did not say it at the meeting. We did not discuss those matters, but just the general situation, the general state of affairs in the military police and his vision as to what it should be like, what the military police should be like, and I agreed completely with him.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, Colonel, Blaskic had the power to direct your organisation to investigate a particular crime; isn't that so?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO PALAVRA
utterances.text: Yes, he could have. Colonel Blaskic could have, and any commander, brigade commander, on the basis of knowledge obtained, could order the military police to examine and investigate a case of that kind and then to inform Colonel Blaskic as to the measures undertaken and what is to be undertaken in the future and what is being done. That is how things were done.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In fact, Blaskic could order that an individual be arrested; isn't that so?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO PALAVRA
utterances.text: Colonel Blaskic or any commander could have ordered an investigation to be undertaken, but how can you investigate if the military police does not arrest and take into custody the perpetrator? He could order but he could not influence. Colonel Blaskic could not influence or any other commander could not influence what the police was doing at the time because the police had its own competencies as to what it was doing. And he couldn't say, "I'd like you to shut him up for five, ten," or whatever time. This was done by the court and the military police collecting documents and facts and figures for the military prosecutor and the courts.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, the fact of the matter is that Blaskic's orders or powers were so vast that he could order the arrest of individuals and also order their summary execution, isn't that so, for crimes such as deserting the line?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO PALAVRA
utterances.text: No. There were very few of us up there. No, no, he couldn't have ordered that, and nobody would ever execute those orders because the courts existed, and so it was our task, our duty, to bring the perpetrator to the courts, and it was up to the court to decide what to do. We couldn't do that. Nobody could do that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let me show you Prosecution Exhibit 456/77, if I may, 456/77. Now, Colonel, that's an order of 11 October, 1993 that, I do believe, was given to you as the commander of the 4th Military Police Battalion, signed by Colonel Blaskic -- actually, this is going over to -- it was sent to a Emil Hara in Vares but from Colonel Blaskic, and notes that given "The rising number of soldiers deserting their position and defence lines has resulted in the loss of defended facilities and entire defence lines. In order to prevent such occurrences, I hereby issue the following order: 1) Undertake the following disciplinary measures against any soldiers and their immediate commanders who desert defence lines: a) execution of the unit/soldier; b) unit commanders will be declared traitors of the nation and given the most severe sentence of death by firing squad in front of the unit. 2) All units and soldiers will be notified of this order. 3) This order will come into force immediately and commanders of brigades and independent units will be responsible for its execution." Did you receive this order, Colonel?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO PALAVRA
utterances.text: If it states here that the 4th Battalion got this, then probably yes, but as far as I can see, the disciplinary measures for leaving the defence lines, desertion of defence lines, I don't know if there were any cases. It is like this on paper, but whether there were any cases in the HVO whether a commander shot by firing squad any one of his members, I don't know of any cases. This is what it says on paper, but I don't recall anybody ever having done that, although people did desert the defence lines, but I don't recall any example of commanders shooting -- having shot some member of his unit. I don't remember that. So one thing is what is written, whereas what was done in the units is quite another. Although I repeat again, people did desert defence lines, there was -- there were cases of desertion, but I cannot recall anybody ever being shot.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Blaskic issued this order to shoot deserters in this particular document, and that, would you agree with me, Colonel, would give Colonel Blaskic extremely vast powers to discipline his troops; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO PALAVRA
utterances.text: Commander Blaskic, I once again state that this is the implementation of disciplinary measures. He did not actually name anybody. He just provided for the possibility of doing so. And he said that there must be no desertion. And if he wrote the order, then he knows why he wrote it and the competencies therein. But it just says under A, against all soldiers, any soldiers and their immediate commander who desert defence lines, that the following disciplinary measures should be undertaken. So he proposes that disciplinary measures in fact be taken, and that all the commanders be informed of the contents of the order. But I repeat once again, are there any examples of anybody, a soldier or commander or anybody, being sent before a firing squad? I don't know of any such case.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you think, Colonel, that maybe they were too afraid once they received this order?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO PALAVRA
utterances.text: Well, these are the regions of Vares, the area of Vares, and had they been afraid they would have all died at the defence lines under Muslim attack. And as you know in Vares, everybody was expelled, and had they been afraid, they would not have left defence lines -- everybody fled, so under the impact of the Muslim forces that were attacking them so much.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, tell me, tell me, Colonel, was it important for you to know the identities of the criminals that were in the 4th Military Police Battalion, so you could reform that military battalion? Was it important to know who else was a criminal in the other units, such as the Vitezovi or Zuti, et cetera? Was that important?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO PALAVRA
utterances.text: Yes, of course. And on two occasions they stole my car. They weren't Serbs or Muslims, they were Croats. Precisely when I started clearing up some of these criminal activities, my car was stolen on two occasions and, in the course of a minute or two later, I was to have been killed in the car as well, because explosives were placed in my car and the car exploded.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, in this meeting with Blaskic in early August of 1993, did he mention Ahmici and the involvement of the military police in the massacre in Ahmici? Did he mention that to you?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO PALAVRA
utterances.text: No, he didn't mention it at that meeting. Had he mentioned it at that meeting, I would have said what we discussed at that meeting. However, at that meeting he did not mention Ahmici. He only mentioned the current situation in the military police and that he had a different vision. He explained what kind of a situation he would have liked, and I agreed with him and I agreed that we should carry out that vision of his, and that we should do things accordingly.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Colonel, if members of the military police under your command were involved in Ahmici, wouldn't it be significant for you to know that and for you to ascertain if you had criminals within the military police?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO PALAVRA
utterances.text: Yes, it is important. Of course it's important.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did Blaskic share with you the results of any of his investigations that were conducted by SIS when you went to his meetings, investigations concerning Ahmici?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO PALAVRA
utterances.text: I was not on that case. I don't know. And he didn't say this to me. Although I later found out that the security service was charged with this duty to investigate how this happened and what happened.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, Colonel, you said to us it would be important to know if there were criminals in the military police who had been involved in Ahmici, and your testimony is that Blaskic neither discussed Ahmici nor shared with you any information he had concerning the events in Ahmici; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Mr. President, these are conclusions, and there is repetition too. The witness said that he didn't discuss Ahmici with him --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Yes, I agree with you, Mr. Nobilo. I know that we are going around Ahmici, I know that you are looking for that result, but you've got an answer to your question. I think you have to move onto something else.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let's move ahead to continue with Ahmici concerning the rest of the investigations. And at any time did anybody come to you and ask to interview some of your soldiers, some of the members of the military police that were under your command concerning the events in Ahmici? And if so, who did they interview and who did the interviewing?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO PALAVRA
utterances.text: I did not interview anyone. If anybody did interview people, then it was the crime investigation service, but, I repeat, when I came the situation was such that the military police were at the front lines. They were carrying out their duties there. And at that time there were very few policemen who were actually involved in military police work. Everybody was at the defence lines precisely for that reason, because many Muslim units were attacking the Lasva River Valley. And I said that at that time the Court of law or, rather, the Military Prosecutor's Office was practically paralysed. They were hardly working at all, because you could not bring soldiers in precisely for that reason. Many were at the defence lines. And I explained that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let me show you Defence Exhibit -- excuse me, Prosecution Exhibit 456/73.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Just for your information, I would like to tell you that you -- that the examination in chief lasted for two hours and twenty minutes, and in about ten minutes -- you have about -- in about ten minutes you have reached the same amount of time that was used for the examination in chief. Do you think that you will have finished by about 20 to one?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: I don't think so, Mr. President. I do believe, and I implore the Court to allow me to continue. The answers that have been given in many instances have not been responsive to the questions that I have posed. That has happened on more than one occasion.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Mr. President, we the defence might be more sympathetic if a lot of time hasn't been spent on events in Travnik and other, quite frankly, peripheral matters. And we would ask the Court to hold the Prosecutor to a reasonable period of time, that is, the same period of time spent on direct, and that will incentavise the Prosecutor to go to the heart of the matter and use his time efficiently and effectively.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Mr. President, I asked this witness how many Bosnian Croats were prosecuted for crimes against the Bosnian Muslims four times. I asked him the same question four times, with Your Honour interceding after the third occasion saying, please, you didn't get a responsive answer, ask the question again.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Yes, but there is something that you have to know, Mr. Kehoe, and that is that the Judges at the proper time will do their own work, they will do their analyses and study what the answers were that were given or that were not given. The Judges will do that. I want to consult with my colleague for a moment. Mr. Kehoe, the Trial Chamber will give you until 1.00, we will resume at 3.00, and if you haven't finished, the Tribunal will give you another 20 to 30 minutes, but no more than that. All right?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: But in general I would like to repeat that in the future try to be sure that the cross-examination does not take longer than the examination in chief. These, of course, are rules that the Judges try to apply with a certain degree of flexibility. All right. Go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. If we can show the witness Exhibit 456/73.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Colonel, this is a document that's in evidence in the -- dated 31 August 1993. It's a communique from the information -- the Information Office of the Central Bosnian Operative Zone.
